question.text: A 27-year-old woman, who recently immigrated from Bangladesh, presents to her primary care physician to discuss birth control. During a review of her past medical history, she reports that as a child she had a recurrent sore throat and fever followed by swollen and aching hip and knee joints. These symptoms returned every season and were never treated but went away on their own only to return with the next typhoon season. When asked about any current complaints, the patient says that she sometimes has shortness of breath and palpitations that do not last long. A physical exam is performed. In which of the auscultation sites will a murmur most likely be heard in this patient?

ARF can lead to rheumatic heart disease (RHD), most commonly affecting the mitral valve, causing mitral regurgitation. The murmur associated with mitral regurgitation is typically a holosystolic murmur heard best at the cardiac apex (Point 3), which may radiate to the axilla. The patient's current symptoms of shortness of breath and palpitations could be related to underlying RHD and mitral regurgitation. Therefore, the murmur is most likely heard at the apex.

Some panelists focused on the apex (Point 3), while others suggested Point 1 (tricuspid area) or Point 2 (pulmonic area), or even Point 4 (left sternal border). The lack of consensus highlights the need for a clear understanding of the typical auscultation findings in RHD.
